demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette:
Adaeze is a 23-year-old Nigerian-American environmental scientist who presented for therapy approximately eight months after the sudden death of her younger brother, Emeka, who was twenty years old at the time. Emeka collapsed at home from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia on a Saturday afternoon in early spring - a day Adaeze has returned to in her mind so many times that the memory has worn grooves she cannot stop falling into. She had been out that day, attending a professional conference two hours from home. She had considered not going. She remembers, with a precision that feels punishing, that Emeka had texted her that morning asking if she wanted to watch a film together, and she had replied that she would be back by evening. She was not back by evening. By the time she arrived home, he was already gone.

In the weeks that followed, Adaeze's grief took on a particular shape that she could not easily name, even to herself. She found herself unable to fully reconstruct the events of that day without something in her pulling back from the edge, as though the full picture were a ledge she could not afford to reach. When she tried to speak about what had happened - to her mother, to a friend who called from Lagos - she would open her mouth and find that the words simply were not there. Not that she had forgotten. She knew exactly what had happened. But the knowledge sat somewhere below language, and she could not retrieve it in any form that felt communicable. More unsettling still was the way the memory, when it did surface, did not feel like a memory at all. She would be in the middle of something ordinary - reviewing water quality data at her desk, or standing at the kettle - and Emeka's absence would arrive not as a thought about the past but as an immediate, present-tense fact, as though she were still in the moment of being told, still standing in the hallway of her parents' house with her coat on.

Adaeze had come to believe, with a conviction she experienced as self-evident rather than as interpretation, that she was the reason her brother died. Not in any abstract sense, but specifically: she should have been there. Someone else, she felt certain, would have called emergency services in time, would have known what to do, would not have been two hours away at a conference that, in retrospect, seemed to her to represent something damning about her priorities. She also held a broader, quieter belief that the event had found her because of who she was - someone who, when it mattered, was absent. Alongside this ran a simmering sense of injustice that had no clear object. Emeka's arrhythmia had been undetected; no one had flagged it, no one had been held accountable, and the world had simply continued. She found this intolerable.

At work, where she spends long hours in the field and in the office conducting environmental impact assessments, delays became a particular source of dread. When a colleague was late returning from a site visit, or when a scheduled call did not connect on time, her body would respond before she had finished forming a single coherent thought - pulse quickening, chest tightening - as though lateness itself had become a signal she was no longer able to interpret as neutral. She stopped watching television almost entirely, avoiding news programmes and drama alike, and when a colleague mentioned a documentary about sudden cardiac events, she left the room without explanation. She began picking arguments with people at work and with friends - small provocations that escalated quickly - and though she could not always explain why, the conflict seemed to offer a kind of noise that temporarily displaced something quieter and worse. Her sleep had become unreliable, and months of exhaustion had begun to affect the quality of her fieldwork reports, something her supervisor had gently raised.

What finally brought Adaeze to seek help was a performance review in which her supervisor expressed concern, and the recognition that she had not spoken Emeka's name aloud in six weeks. What she is most afraid of, she said in her first session, is that if she actually looks at what happened - all of it, clearly - she will find that it confirms everything she already suspects about herself. What she hopes for, more tentatively, is that it might not.
